anatomy.lede: The largest animal on land is built around a few extraordinary tools: a trunk that is both nose and hand, ears that work as radiators, and teeth that are replaced from the back of the jaw like a conveyor belt.

hotspots.label: Ear
hotspots.text: The huge triangular ears help the elephant keep cool in the hottest months.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Long lashes guard the small eyes from dust and debris. Elephants see in two colour channels, much like a red–green colour-blind person.

hotspots.label: Tusk
hotspots.text: Tusks are enlarged incisor teeth made of ivory. Calves are born without them; the tusk-forming incisors replace small milk teeth at about a year old.

hotspots.label: Trunk
hotspots.text: The muscular trunk is used for breathing, smelling and grabbing objects, and as a temporary container to suck up water and squirt it into the mouth.

hotspots.label: Cracked skin
hotspots.text: A network of tiny cracks covers the skin. These channels hold water and mud, helping the elephant stay cool and protecting it from parasites and sun.

hotspots.label: Foot
hotspots.text: Some of a rumble's energy travels through the ground. Elephants detect these seismic calls and can tell those of familiar and unfamiliar herds apart.

hotspots.label: Calf
hotspots.text: A newborn weighs about 100 kg. It stays close at its mother's side for its first four years or so.

senses.lede: An elephant lives in a world of smell and sound — much of it below the range of human hearing — and even feels distant calls through the ground.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: African elephants carry about 2,000 working smell-receptor genes, packed into enlarged gene clusters — an extreme expansion compared with the other mammals studied.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Much of an adult's rumble lies below about 20 Hz, under the lower limit of human hearing, yet elephants respond to such calls played from kilometres away.

senses.name: Seismic sense
senses.text: Part of a rumble's energy travels through the ground. In playback trials, wild elephants reacted to seismic alarm calls of familiar herds but ignored those of strangers.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Elephants have two colour pigments in daylight, sensitive to blue and yellow-green light, giving them dichromatic vision like a red–green colour-blind person.

senses.name: Touch
senses.text: Touch matters most between mother and calf and between mating pairs; courting elephants stroke each other with their trunks.

body.lede: Keeping a six-tonne body fed, cool and working for 60 years or more takes some unusual engineering.

systems.title: Six sets of molars
systems.text: Elephants grow six molars on each side of each jaw in turn. Each new tooth moves forward as the one in front wears away; when the sixth is worn down there is no replacement, and the elephant can no longer chew its food.

systems.title: Skin that cracks on purpose
systems.text: The outer layer of elephant skin is thick, brittle and slow to shed. As it thickens on the skin's tiny bumps it fractures, creating micrometre-wide channels that hold water and mud.

systems.title: Ears as radiators
systems.text: The large ears help keep the body cool. Elephants also use their trunks to coat themselves with mud or water, which helps them stay hydrated.

systems.title: A trunk for drinking
systems.text: An elephant needs around 50 gallons (about 190 litres) of water every day. It sucks water into its trunk and squirts it into its mouth rather than drinking directly.

genome.lede: A first draft of the African elephant genome was released in 2009, and a chromosome-level assembly followed in 2023. It has helped explain why such a large, long-lived animal rarely gets cancer.

findings.title: Twenty copies of a cancer guard
findings.text: Humans have one copy of the tumour-suppressor gene TP53; African elephants have at least 20, most of them extra copies called retrogenes. Elephant cells exposed to DNA damage self-destruct more readily than human cells, and elephants' estimated cancer mortality is about 5%, against 11–25% in people.

findings.title: A zombie gene comes back to life
findings.text: Elephants revived a dead copy of a gene called LIF6. Switched on by TP53 when DNA is damaged, it helps kill the damaged cell — a change that appeared as elephants' ancestors grew large.

findings.title: Two species, long apart
findings.text: Genomes from living and extinct elephants show the ancestors of savanna and forest elephants were almost completely isolated from each other for about 500,000 years, supporting their treatment as separate species.

mind.lede: Long lives, long memories and close family ties make elephants some of the most socially skilled animals studied.

studies.title: The wisdom of the matriarch
studies.text: Playback experiments in Amboseli, Kenya, showed that families led by older matriarchs were better at telling familiar callers from strangers, and these groups may raise more calves.

studies.title: Reading a pointing finger
studies.text: Eleven captive African elephants, without prior training, found hidden food by following a person's pointing gesture, even when the gesture was subtle.

studies.title: Telling people apart by voice
studies.text: In Amboseli, family groups bunched defensively and sniffed the air more after hearing recorded voices of Maasai men, who pose a greater threat to them, than voices of another ethnic group — and reacted less to Maasai women and boys.

studies.title: Calling each other by name
studies.text: Machine-learning analysis of wild elephant rumbles found calls specific to the elephant being addressed, and elephants reacted more strongly to playbacks of calls originally aimed at them.

survival.lede: A healthy adult has little to fear from other animals. The danger is to calves that stray — and, above all, from people.

tactics.title: Safety in the herd
tactics.text: Females live in family herds of 6 to 70 animals that guard the young. Predators mostly take calves that lag behind the group.

tactics.title: Sheer size
tactics.text: Males can weigh over six tonnes. Few predators will risk attacking a full-grown elephant.

tactics.title: Long-distance warning
tactics.text: Elephants call to warn or gather members of their herd, and their low-frequency calls can be heard by other elephants at least 4 km away.

threats.title: Poaching for ivory
threats.text: Despite an international ban on the ivory trade since 1989, illegal ivory trading doubled between 2007 and 2014.

threats.title: Losing the oldest
threats.text: Hunters often target the largest elephants. Because older females hold the herd's social knowledge, losing them may harm the whole family.

threats.title: Shrinking, unprotected range
threats.text: About 70% of the elephant's remaining range lies outside protected land, and human development continues to take habitat.

life.lede: Elephants grow up slowly, with the longest pregnancy of any land mammal and years of learning within the family.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: A single calf, rarely twins, develops for almost two years. Females breed only once every 3 to 9 years.

stages.name: Newborn
stages.text: The calf weighs 90–120 kg at birth. It may suckle for up to three years and keeps close to its mother, who helps it past obstacles.

stages.name: Youngster
stages.text: The whole herd teaches the young elephant to use its trunk, find food and move safely, until it becomes independent at around eight.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females mature at about 11 and stay with their family; males mature at about 20 and live alone or with a few other bulls.

lifespan.value: 60–70 years on average in the wild
